stances.claim: If and when the US requests Quiboloy's extradition, the Philippines 'will have no choice but to follow the Extradition Treaty,' just as it did in the Mark Jimenez case.

Extradition has two phases: an executive evaluation (DFA) and a judicial extradition hearing (RTC). The wanted person is NOT entitled to due process at the evaluation phase because he is not yet at risk of arrest -- only the RTC determines whether a warrant should issue.

one_paragraph_summary: The US Treasury's Dec. 10 (Human Rights Day) sanctions on Apollo C. Quiboloy -- founder and self-proclaimed 'Appointed Son of God' of the Kingdom of Jesus Christ -- for alleged human-rights violations and other offenses freeze his and KJC's US properties and bar US persons from transacting with him. Quiboloy was no longer in the US when the sanctions hit, and he has claimed in local media that the sanctions deprived him of human rights for lack of notice and due process. While no extradition request has been made, Panganiban revisits how one would proceed under the RP-US Extradition Treaty (signed Nov. 13, 1994; Senate-ratified) and the Mark Jimenez precedent. Extradition has two phases: a Phase 1 executive evaluation by the DFA of the requesting state's documentation, and a Phase 2 judicial hearing where the DFA and DOJ file the extradition charge in an RTC, which decides. In Secretary of Justice v. Lantion (Jan. 18, 2000), the Court initially ruled 9-6 -- Justice Melo's ponencia, joined by Bellosillo, Vitug, Kapunan, Quisumbing, Purisima, Buena, Santiago, and De Leon -- that Jimenez was entitled to notice and copies during Phase 1 because under the Treaty the US could request provisional arrest 'in case of urgency,' putting him at risk of deprivation of liberty. Justice (later CJ) Puno and Panganiban dissented, joined by CJ Davide and Justices Mendoza, Pardo, and Reyes, arguing that the DFA only checks documents while the RTC alone issues warrants. On Oct. 17, 2000 -- same 9-6 vote, with Quisumbing, Purisima, and De Leon 'somersaulting' -- the Court reversed itself and adopted the dissents: an extradition case is not criminal in nature; its purpose is merely to determine whether the wanted person should be surrendered to face the charges abroad with all the constitutional rights of the accused. Jimenez eventually faced US criminal proceedings. Though a congressman and close to both Arroyo and Estrada, neither president intervened -- protecting diplomatic relations with America. Quiboloy's alleged offenses (human rights, dollar trafficking, rape of young KJC women) materially exceed Jimenez's (a prohibited foreign donation to Bill Clinton's campaign), so if and when a request comes, the Philippines 'will have no choice but to follow the Extradition Treaty,' just as it did with Jimenez.
